title: Southern Italy's Treasury of Native Grapes
quiz.0.question: Why is Primitivo called that?
quiz.0.explanation: The name Primitivo comes from the Italian "primo" (first, foremost), because it is one of Puglia's earliest-ripening varieties (late August to early September).
quiz.1.question: What does the name Negroamaro mean?
quiz.1.options.1: Latin niger (black) + Greek mavro (black) = double black
quiz.1.explanation: The most common explanation is Negroamaro = Latin "niger" (black) + Greek "mavro" (black), meaning "double black", reflecting the grape's very deep colour; another theory derives it from the Italian negro (black) + amaro (bitter).
quiz.2.question: What is the blend of Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG?
quiz.2.explanation: Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG (Sicily's only DOCG) blends Nero d'Avola 50-70% (structure, colour) + Frappato 30-50% (aroma, elegance, acidity).
quiz.3.question: Why did the Romans call Fiano Vitis Apiana?
quiz.3.options.0: It came from the Apianum area
quiz.3.options.1: Apis = bee; bees particularly loved this sweet grape
quiz.3.explanation: The Romans called Fiano Vitis Apiana (from apis = bee) because when ripe it is high in sugar and intensely aromatic, attracting swarms of bees.

slides.2.title: 🍇 Primitivo — Grape Profile & DNA Revealed
slides.2.content:
"Primo" = first to ripen, Puglia's earliest-picked grape — DNA research from the 1990s onwards proved that Primitivo = Zinfandel = Crljenak Kaštelanski (confirmed in 2001): one variety, but very different styles

📊

Grape Profile

Name: "Primitivo" = "primo" (first to ripen)

Ripening: very early (late August to early September, Puglia's earliest harvest)

Alcohol: 14-16% (builds sugar easily, with uneven ripening within a bunch)

Colour: deep purple-black (very high in anthocyanins)

Flavours: black cherry jam, plum, blackberry, spice, liquorice, chocolate

Plantings: in Italy almost entirely in Puglia, best known in Manduria and Gioia del Colle

🏆

Two Styles from Manduria

Primitivo di Manduria Dolce Naturale DOCG (sweet):
A DOCG since 2011, a naturally sweet (unfortified) wine high in both alcohol and residual sugar, rich and jammy; pair with chocolate desserts and blue cheese

Primitivo di Manduria DOC (dry):
Dry and full-bodied, 14-16% alcohol, ageing potential of 5-10 years; often more mineral and savoury than Californian Zinfandel

slides.3.title: ⚔️ Primitivo vs Zinfandel — Same Blood, Two Souls
slides.3.content:
The same DNA, very different styles — originating in Croatia (Crljenak Kaštelanski), the Italian version wins with minerality and elegance, the Californian with jammy richness

🇮🇹 Primitivo (Puglia) — Elegant Minerality

Where: around Manduria, province of Taranto, a hot, dry Mediterranean climate

Style: elegant, mineral and savoury, with more Mediterranean sense of place than the Californian version

Alcohol: 14-16% (slightly lower than Zinfandel)

Character: black fruit and spice + clear savoury minerality + a strong sense of place

Winemaking: some traditional large-cask ageing; the sweet Dolce Naturale is a speciality

Appellations: Primitivo di Manduria DOC, Gioia del Colle DOC

🇺🇸 Zinfandel (California) — Jammy Richness

Where: Sonoma Dry Creek Valley / Napa / Lodi (across California)

Style: jammy, explosively fruity, sweet spice, usually with less of the Italian minerality

Alcohol: 15-17% (California's abundant sunshine gives higher alcohol)

Character: black fruit + sweet spice + clear oak influence, a rich palate

Special: White Zinfandel (a sweet rosé) is a mass-market American speciality

Old vines: California preserves many Zinfandel vines over a century old

slides.4.title: ⚫ Negroamaro — "Double Black"
slides.4.content:
Latin niger (black) + Greek mavro (black) = double black — the star grape of Puglia's Salento peninsula, drought- and heat-tolerant and suited to the hot south; in 1943 it made Italy's first commercial rosé, a historic first

📊 Grape Profile

Colour: deep purple-black (very high in anthocyanins, truly "double black")

Tannin: medium to high (soft, not as astringent as Sagrantino)

Acidity: medium

Alcohol: 13-15%

Flavours: black cherry, plum, blackberry, herbs, liquorice, tobacco, chocolate

Character: drought- and heat-tolerant, perfectly adapted to Puglia's hot, dry climate

🏆 Main Appellations & the Five Roses Legend

Salice Salentino DOC: Negroamaro-based, the best-known of the Salento peninsula, fruity, soft and easy, with a Riserva level

Copertino DOC: Negroamaro-based, more structured, with ageing potential

🌸 Five Roses (1943):
Leone De Castris made Italy's first commercial rosato from Negroamaro, pale pink and fresh; the name comes from the estate's Cinque Rose area, switched to the English "Five Roses" at the request of Allied general Charles Poletti; still one of Puglia's most famous rosatos

slides.5.title: 🌋 Nero d'Avola — King of Sicily
slides.5.content:
"The black one from Avola", Sicily's most important red grape — once used for bulk production and export, it gained international recognition after the 1990s quality revolution led by Planeta, Donnafugata and others; it is at its best in its south-eastern homeland of Noto and Pachino

📊 Grape Profile

Colour: deep purple-black

Tannin: medium to high

Acidity: medium

Alcohol: 13.5-15%

Flavours: black cherry, black plum, blackberry, spice, chocolate, liquorice, tobacco

Structure: full-bodied with intense fruit

Regional differences: south-east Noto/Pachino (elegant, mineral, savoury) / Etna volcano (high acid, fine and complex) / the west (rich and high in alcohol)

🔄 Quality Revolution & Blends

Traditional (before 1980): bulk production, exported to France and northern Italy to deepen colour, ordinary quality

Modern (after 1990): low yields + French oak + investment by estates such as Planeta and Donnafugata, high-quality single-varietal wines

Blends:
Nero d'Avola + Syrah (more spicy complexity)
Nero d'Avola + Cabernet (more structure for ageing)
Nero d'Avola + Frappato = Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG (Sicily's only DOCG)

slides.6.title: 🌸 Frappato & Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG
slides.6.content:
A light, aromatic red grape from south-east Sicily, a natural-wine favourite — Frappato and Nero d'Avola join to create Cerasuolo di Vittoria (Sicily's only DOCG, 2005), two complementary personalities in perfect balance

🌸 Frappato Grape Profile

Colour: light to medium red (paler than Nero d'Avola, near garnet)

Tannin: low to medium (silky and smooth)

Acidity: high

Alcohol: 12-13.5%

Flavours: red cherry, strawberry, raspberry, violet, rose, spice

Character: aromatic, elegant, light and easy, called "Italy's Pinot Noir"

Natural wine: natural producers such as Arianna Occhipinti and COS love this grape

🏆 Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG

Sicily's only DOCG (established 2005)

The golden blend:
Nero d'Avola 50-70% (structure, colour, tannin)
Frappato 30-50% (aroma, elegance, acidity)

Style: balanced and elegant, fruity, medium-bodied, silky tannins

Flavours: red fruit + spice + florals

Release: the standard wine after 1 June of the year following harvest; Classico after 31 March of the second year after harvest; most are best within 3-5 years

slides.7.title: 🏺 Fiano — The Romans' Vitis Apiana
slides.7.content:
The "grape loved by bees" recorded by the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder — when ripe, Fiano is high in sugar and intensely aromatic, attracting swarms of bees; Fiano di Avellino DOCG, on high volcanic soils, can after 5-15 years of ageing rival great white wines in complexity

📊

Grape Profile

Acidity: medium to high

Body: medium to full

Alcohol: 12.5-14%

Flavours (young): white peach, apricot, pear, white flowers, almond, lemon

Flavours (aged): honey, beeswax, hazelnut, minerality, spice, smoke

Ageing potential: 5-15 years

Name: Vitis Apiana (apis = bee), because it attracts bees when ripe

🏆

Fiano di Avellino DOCG

Location: the hills of the inland province of Avellino, Campania

Elevation: 400-700 m (high elevation preserves acidity)

Soils: volcanic tuff (giving a distinctive minerality)

Grape: 85%+ Fiano

Style: very mineral (from the volcanic soils), full and complex, rivalling great white Burgundy with age

Producers: Feudi di San Gregorio / Mastroberardino

Neighbouring DOCGs: Greco di Tufo, Taurasi

slides.8.title: 🇬🇷 Greco — Legacy of the Greek Colonists
slides.8.content:
A grape traditionally believed to have been brought to southern Italy by Greek colonists — the volcanic tuff (tufo) soils of Greco di Tufo DOCG give an explosive minerality; Calabria also has the rare sweet Greco di Bianco, one of southern Italy's most precious sweet wines

📊 Greco Profile & Greco di Tufo DOCG

Acidity: very high

Body: full

Alcohol: 12.5-14%

Flavours: lemon, green apple, white peach, almond, minerality, herbs, saltiness

Character: very mineral (volcanic tuff soils), ageing potential of 8-15 years

DOCG: around the village of Tufo in the province of Avellino, Campania, where tuff and sulphur-bearing layers give a vivid minerality

Pairing: oysters, seafood, mozzarella di bufala

🍯 Greco di Bianco DOC — Calabria's Sweet Treasure

Method: grapes dried until the sugar is highly concentrated (passito)

Grape: the local Greco Bianco, not the same variety as the Greco of Greco di Tufo

Style: high in both alcohol and residual sugar

Flavours: dried apricot, honey, fig, caramel, citrus peel

Production: tiny (a rare treasure)

History: the village of Bianco at the southern tip of Calabria, an ancient sweet-wine tradition

slides.9.title: 🏛️ Falanghina — A Roman Legacy
slides.9.content:
Possibly a descendant of the grape behind Falernum, ancient Rome's most famous wine — it declined in the 20th century and, once promoted again, became one of Campania's most popular white grapes; two styles: complex and mineral from the volcanic Naples area vs fruity and floral from inland Benevento

📊 Grape Profile & Two Styles

Acidity: medium to high

Body: light to medium

Alcohol: 12-13.5%

Flavours: lemon, green apple, white flowers, almond, herbs, minerality

Flegrea (volcanic): Campi Flegrei DOC (west of Naples), volcanic soils, very mineral, clearly savoury, complex in structure

Beneventana (Sannio): inland province of Benevento, fruity, fresh and floral, easy and approachable, larger volumes

🏛️ The Falernum Legend & the Revival

Roman legend: Falernum was ancient Rome's most expensive and admired wine, praised by Pliny the Elder and the poet Horace, and famous for its longevity

The Falanghina link: possibly a descendant of Falernum's grape (no DNA proof, but geography and taste fit)

Late 20th century: it declined, and from the 1970s Campania estates promoted it again, so plantings gradually recovered

Today: one of Campania's most popular white grapes, its reputation rising fast

slides.10.title: 📊 Southern Grapes Compared
slides.10.content:
🔍 A Guide to Southern Italian Grapes

Southern Italy's grapes span four regions — Puglia, Campania, Sicily and Calabria — with vivid red and white personalities. Common themes: volcanic soils bring minerality (Fiano/Greco/Falanghina) and hot climates create dark, high-alcohol reds (Primitivo/Negroamaro/Nero d'Avola).

🍷 The Four Southern Reds

Primitivo (= Zinfandel by DNA, 14-16%, very early-ripening, Puglia) ✦ Negroamaro (niger + mavro, double black, Salento, Italy's first commercial rosato in 1943) ✦ Nero d'Avola (king of Sicily, 1990s quality revolution, best in the south-east) ✦ Frappato (Sicily's Pinot Noir, the soul of Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG)

⚪ Campania's Big Three Whites

Fiano (Vitis Apiana, the Romans' bee grape, Avellino volcanic soils, ages 5-15 years) ✦ Greco (a Greek legacy, explosive tuff minerality, a dry DOCG + a rare sweet passito) ✦ Falanghina (a descendant of Roman Falernum?, complex volcanic Flegrea vs fruity, easy Beneventana)

⚠️ Southern Essentials to Remember

Sicily's only DOCG = Cerasuolo di Vittoria (Nero d'Avola 50-70% + Frappato 30-50%). Primitivo's trinity: = Zinfandel = Crljenak Kaštelanski (confirmed by DNA, originating in Croatia). Campania's three whites (Fiano/Greco/Falanghina): volcanic tuff is their shared source of minerality.

slides.11.points.3: ✓ Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most important red grape, internationally recognised after the 1990s quality revolution; blended with Frappato it makes Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG (Sicily's only DOCG, 2005)

slides.11.points.5: ✓ Fiano was called Vitis Apiana (loved by bees) by the Romans; Fiano di Avellino DOCG, on Campania's high volcanic soils (400-700 m), can age 5-15 years and rival great whites

slides.11.points.7: ✓ Falanghina's two styles: Flegrea (volcanic, west of Naples, complex and mineral) vs Beneventana (Benevento, fruity, floral and easy); possibly a descendant of Rome's most expensive wine, Falernum
